title: Silence at home
hookLine: a loud kitchen, and two old answers to whether quiet can live there
tomorrow: before the first bite, what did monks stop to think?

lines: A HUM, A CALL, A TV.
cards: A dishwasher hums. Someone's on a work call in the next room. A TV is on that nobody is watching.

In a busy house, can real quiet live there at all? The suttas give two answers, and both are worth hearing. One says the household life is crowded and dusty, and the life gone forth is like the open air.
The other points to householders who found deep stillness without ever leaving home. Two views, one kitchen, and a house that isn't going to get any emptier this week.

teach.h: CITTA: STILLNESS IN A BUSY LIFE.
teach.b: In the suttas, people who leave home often say the same thing before they go: household life is crowded, a road of dust; going forth is wide open.

It's hard, living at home, to keep the holy life complete and polished like a shell. On this view, the forest and the monastery exist for a reason. Silence at home is a small thing, and it's honest to say so.
Nobody in those stories is running away from a family; they want the whole day for practice, not just its edges. Second view.
The suttas also tell of Citta, a householder with a business and a town to answer to, who says he can enter deep meditation, at will, as far as the fourth jhana. Nobody sends him to the forest.
Lay followers in the texts keep observance days at home, with fewer words and simpler food.

teach.h: TALK OF DHAMMA, OR NOBLE SILENCE.
teach.b: And the Buddha's advice to his monks when they gather fits any room: talk about the Dhamma, or keep noble silence. Here's the fair way to hold both.
The first view doesn't say home is worthless; it says leaving gives the practice more room. The second doesn't say leaving is pointless; it says stillness isn't locked inside a monastery.
Both agree that quiet is made, not found.
Quiet at home won't be a forest. It can still be ten minutes the house agrees to keep.

how: Some Buddhist families keep a short daily quiet time at a home shrine, and lay Buddhists often keep observance days with fewer words and simpler meals; monastics keep longer silences in the monastery.

o: a short quiet a household makes together, noise and all
a vow never to speak again, kept for life
moving out to a monastery to find real stillness

games.q: two views on quiet — tap the pairs.
p: wide open, like the open air
what monks keep when not talking Dhamma

s: the suttas say a householder can't meditate deeply
Citta, a householder, says he can enter the fourth jhana at will.
people leaving home in the suttas call household life crowded and dusty
and going forth wide open, like the open air.
the Buddha's advice: talk about the Dhamma, or keep noble silence.

games.q: a friend says quiet at home is pointless; real stillness needs a retreat. give her view its best case before you answer.
o: she's right that leaving gives practice more room; the suttas say home is crowded.
she's just making excuses not to practice at home.
she's wrong; the suttas say home is exactly as good as the forest.
games.why: her view is in the suttas: household life is crowded and dusty. Citta's story is the other side: stillness can be made at home too.

practice: Listen for one sound in the house, the fridge, a fan, traffic far off, and stay with that one sound. When others come, let them be part of the room without chasing them.
Let the noise stay, and let your listening be the quiet part, the one corner of the house that is still.

wordCard.voice: Silence at home: quiet made inside an ordinary house, small and real, not waiting for a forest.

orig.note: Pali: mona, silence; a muni is a silent sage.

carryVoice: Carry this: quiet at home is made, a few minutes at a time. Six of nine.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2 and Majjhima Nikaya 36 (the going-forth reflection: household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is wide open)
Samyutta Nikaya 41.9 (Citta the householder says he can enter the four jhanas)
Majjhima Nikaya 26 (when gathered, either talk on the Dhamma or keep noble silence)
